nautical mile.definition: A nautical mile is a unit of distance equal to exactly 1,852 meters, tied to one minute of latitude and used worldwide in maritime and aviation navigation.

knot.definition: A knot is a unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour (1.852 km/h). Marine wind, boat speed, and current are usually given in knots.

fathom.definition: A fathom is six feet (1.8288 m), traditionally used for depth soundings and anchor rode in some regions.

great circle.definition: A great circle is the shortest path between two points on a sphere; long ocean routes are often planned as great-circle tracks with rhumb-line legs for practical steering.

bearing.definition: A bearing is a direction expressed as an angle, usually clockwise from north (true or magnetic), used to describe courses and relative positions.

dead reckoning.definition: Dead reckoning estimates position from a known fix using course and distance (or speed and time) without new observations; it ignores set and drift unless adjusted to an estimated position.

apparent wind.definition: Apparent wind is the wind felt on a moving vessel: the vector sum of true wind and wind created by the boat’s motion through the air.

true wind.definition: True wind is the wind relative to the fixed water or land surface, before the boat’s motion alters what an observer feels.

anchor scope.definition: Anchor scope is the ratio of deployed rode length to vertical depth at the bow; higher scope generally improves holding until swinging room becomes limiting.

Beaufort scale.definition: The Beaufort scale classifies wind strength by observed sea state and wind speed bands, giving mariners a common language for conditions.

significant wave height.definition: Significant wave height is approximately the average height of the highest one-third of waves in a sea state, not the largest single wave.

hull speed.definition: Hull speed is a practical speed ceiling for many displacement hulls, often approximated from waterline length; it is not a hard physical limit for all vessels.

VMG.definition: Velocity made good (VMG) is the component of the boat’s speed toward or away from a mark or waypoint, critical for upwind and downwind tactics.

rhumb line.definition: A rhumb line crosses meridians at a constant bearing; it is simpler to steer than a great circle but is not the shortest path on the globe.

nautical chart.definition: A nautical chart is a map for navigation showing depths, aids, hazards, and often magnetic variation; distances are read with the latitude scale for nautical miles.
